summary: The developer machine has everything required to start building the Node.js (Mongoose) hospital-bed occupancy sample against the live Azure DocumentDB cluster: Node, npx, Docker, the documentdb MCP server and a comprehensive set of documentdb-* skills are installed, and az is signed in. Key factual confusions in the cold answers were resolved using the installed DocumentDB skills and Microsoft Learn pages (notably: resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters, capacity is vCore tiers not RUs, the service supports Microsoft Entra ID, change streams are supported, and the service exposes vector and integrated search features). Missing accelerators (DocumentDB Agent Kit package and a local gateway/mongosh) and a few documentation ambiguities remain; they do not block coding but will slow manual verification and local interactive checks.
summary_points: Ready to start: Node 24, npm/npx, az (signed in), docker, 'documentdb' MCP server and many documentdb-* skills are present so code and verification against the live cluster can begin.

Major cold-answer confusions were corrected: the resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not databaseAccounts), capacity is vCore/compute tiers (M10..M200) not RU-based, and the service supports Microsoft Entra ID and change streams (with feature toggle for some multishard scenarios).

DocumentDB-specific features (vector indexes, integrated full-text / $search, TTL/index patterns) are supported — use the documentdb-vector-search, documentdb-full-text-search and documentdb-indexing skills and the Learn pages referenced below.

Missing developer conveniences (mongosh, a single 'DocumentDB Agent Kit' accelerator entry, bicep/terraform/azd on PATH) would speed tests and infra work; they are not strictly blocking but are recommended.

One factual ambiguity remains (TTL semantics for arbitrary Date-field TTL vs service _ts-based TTL) — the service supports TTL indexes and expireAfterSeconds; prefer explicit Date-field TTL indexes for per-document expiry and validate behavior on the target cluster.
Verdict: ready_with_gaps — proceed to implement the sample, using the documented workarounds and the installed skills for correctness and verification.

tools.name: node
tools.needed_for: Run the Node.js/Mongoose sample, npm install, npx.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run or build the sample; Node is required for any Node.js sample.
tools.workaround: Install Node.js 24. Use Node version manager (nvm) if needed.

tools.name: npx / npm
tools.needed_for: bootstrap scripts, installing any MCP skill helpers, running project npm scripts.
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to run developer helper scripts and to install optional skills; would require global installs.
tools.workaround: Install npm / npx (bundled with Node) or run scripts via yarn if available.

tools.name: az
tools.needed_for: Inspect Azure resources, verify provider registration and (if needed) retrieve cluster connection info or resource metadata.
tools.detail: azure-cli 2.89.1, signed in to a subscription
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot inspect or register Azure providers or retrieve resource metadata; deployment troubleshooting is harder.
tools.workaround: Use the documentdb MCP server or portal for read-only cluster metadata if az is unavailable.

tools.name: docker
tools.needed_for: Optionally run a local DocumentDB gateway image for local integration testing.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run local gateway container; must test against live cluster.
tools.workaround: Build and test against the live cluster (DOCUMENTDB_URI) as the prompt instructs.

tools.name: azd
tools.needed_for: Optional: template-based app deploys with Azure Developer CLI.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot use azd-based scaffolds; not required for this Node sample.
tools.workaround: Use npm scripts and az (or Bicep / Terraform when added) for any infra/deploy tasks; add azd if the team prefers azd flows.

tools.name: bicep
tools.needed_for: Optional: generate and test Bicep deployment templates (documentdb-azure-deployment recommends Bicep).
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot author/run Bicep locally from PATH; slows IaC-oriented builders who want to include cluster templates.
tools.workaround: Use the Bicep templates shipped in the documentdb-azure-deployment skill examples or use az resource create with api-version as shown in the skill.

tools.name: terraform
tools.needed_for: Optional: Terraform deployment and IaC examples (documentdb-azure-deployment includes Terraform samples).
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run Terraform-based provisioning locally; not required for this sample because an existing cluster is used.
tools.workaround: Use Bicep/az resource create examples inside documentdb-azure-deployment, or add Terraform if IaC is desired later.

tools.name: mongosh
tools.needed_for: Interactive Mongo shell to inspect collections, indexes and run quick manual queries against the cluster.
tools.impact_if_missing: Slows manual interactive verification; the documentdb MCP server can run equivalent reads, but mongosh is the fastest way to sanity-check indexes and sample documents locally.
tools.workaround: Use the 'documentdb' MCP server tools (documentdb_find_documents / documentdb_list_indexes / documentdb_get_statistics) to inspect collections and indexes.

tools.name: git
tools.needed_for: Source control for the sample repository.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot version files locally; not blocking for a single dev but recommended.
tools.workaround: Use zip/tar snapshots; install git for normal workflow.

tools.name: documentdb (MCP server)
tools.needed_for: Data-plane inspection and verification (list databases/collections, sample documents, create/list/drop indexes, run aggregate/explain). Required to inspect the live cluster from the agent.
tools.detail: 18 read-only tools available (documentdb_list_databases, documentdb_create_index, documentdb_list_indexes, documentdb_explain_operation, etc.). Use connection_profile "default".
tools.impact_if_missing: Agent could not inspect the cluster or verify indexes/collections programmatically. Manual checks via mongosh/portal would be required.
tools.workaround: Use mongosh or the Azure Portal to inspect cluster state if MCP server absent.

tools.name: learn (Microsoft Learn MCP server)
tools.needed_for: Search & fetch authoritative Microsoft Learn documentation to ground decisions and verify cold answers.
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to ground facts; reliance on local skills would increase risk of outdated knowledge.
tools.workaround: Use public docs via a browser or local copies; prefer installing the learn MCP server.

tools.name: Installed documentdb-* skills
tools.needed_for: Authoritative, task-specific guidance (deploy, connection tuning, indexing, vector search, local dev, security). These skills are essential references and provide examples the builder must follow.
tools.detail: Many skills installed: documentdb-azure-deployment, documentdb-connection, documentdb-driver, documentdb-data-modeling, documentdb-indexing, documentdb-local-deployment, documentdb-mcp-setup, documentdb-vector-search, documentdb-full-text-search, documentdb-security, documentdb-monitoring, documentdb-sharding, documentdb-storage, documentdb-natural-language-querying, documentdb-query-optimizer, documentdb-query-optimization, documentdb-high-availability.
tools.impact_if_missing: Without these skills, the builder loses targeted best-practice guidance; building is still possible using Microsoft Learn pages but will be slower and error-prone.
tools.workaround: Rely on Microsoft Learn pages and the documentdb MCP server; install individual skills via the DocumentDB Agent Kit if desired.

accelerators_missed: DocumentDB Agent Kit (single npx package) — not present as a named accelerator; the installed granular skills appear to cover most kit functionality but installing the kit (npx skills add Azure/documentdb-agent-kit) would simplify skill management and provide canonical templates.

Local DocumentDB gateway container (developer Docker image) — Docker is installed but no local gateway is running; running the gateway locally (documentdb-local-deployment guidance) speeds iterative development and offline integration tests.
mongosh (interactive shell) — missing from PATH; installing mongosh speeds manual verification of indexes and sample documents.

Bicep / Terraform on PATH — both are not on PATH; documentdb-azure-deployment recommends Bicep as the primary IaC approach and provides templates; installing Bicep/Terraform would speed infrastructure / template validation and allow local IaC testing.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type: databaseAccounts. In ARM/Bicep you reference it as Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts.
confusions.grounded_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type: mongoClusters (i.e., Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters) — use this resource type for Azure DocumentDB clusters (API examples and Bicep/ARM templates reference mongoClusters).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Shared provider namespace (Microsoft.DocumentDB) and historical use of Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts for Cosmos DB accounts; older Cosmos DB docs and templates still reference databaseAccounts, causing the model to name the databaseAccounts resource type.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder used databaseAccounts and az cosmosdb flows, they would target Cosmos DB 'databaseAccounts' resources instead of the vCore DocumentDB cluster API; Bicep/ARM/az commands would be wrong for provisioning or for any resource-specific property names (shard/compute settings), and some management commands would fail or affect the wrong service.
improvements: On the main Azure DocumentDB quickstart and Bicep templates page, add a one-line note: 'This product uses Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters; do not use Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts for vCore clusters.'
Update the documentdb MCP skill description to explicitly repeat the resource type (Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters) where it describes deployment flows.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the core CLI group az cosmosdb. Example create command: az cosmosdb create ... Mongo-specific subcommands are under az cosmosdb mongodb ... This is part of the main az CLI, not a separate extension.
confusions.grounded_answer: For Azure DocumentDB (vCore / mongoClusters) the recommended paths are: use the Bicep templates (Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters) or az resource create against resource-type 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters' (api-version examples are in the documentdb-azure-deployment skill). There is no dedicated 'az documentdb' core top-level command group for mongoClusters; some Cosmos DB functionality still lives under az cosmosdb for databaseAccounts, but creating a mongoClusters resource is done via resource template/Bicep or az resource create with the mongoClusters resourceType.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Overlap in 'DocumentDB' / 'Cosmos DB' naming and the existence of az cosmosdb command groups for Cosmos DB databaseAccounts; the model assumed the Cosmos CLI group also applies to new mongoClusters resources.
confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb create would create or manage Cosmos DB databaseAccounts (RU-based) instead of the vCore mongoClusters resource; the wrong API surface would be used and properties expected by the sample (compute tier M30, mongo serverVersion 8.0, shard settings) would not match.
improvements: Add a short how-to on the 'Quickstart: Bicep' page showing the az resource create command used for mongoClusters (API 2025-09-01) with an example — this will guide authors away from az cosmosdb.

On the DocumentDB quickstart landing page, add an explicit callout: 'To create vCore DocumentDB clusters, deploy Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (Bicep or az resource create); do not use az cosmosdb databaseAccounts.'

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep/ARM: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts ... Terraform: azurerm_cosmosdb_account ...
confusions.grounded_answer: Bicep/ARM and Terraform deploy the DocumentDB cluster with resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (Bicep/ARM) and the Terraform resource examples target the mongoClusters type (azurerm_mongo_cluster or AzAPI entries that map to Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older templates and common Cosmos DB examples use Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts and azurerm_cosmosdb_account; the new vCore offering uses a different resource type (mongoClusters).
confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong resource type in IaC will fail to deploy a vCore DocumentDB cluster or will create an unintended Cosmos DB account with different billing and API semantics.
improvements: Add a migration note to the 'databaseAccounts' template pages pointing to 'mongoClusters' for vCore DocumentDB customers, and a one-line example of the az resource create command used for mongoClusters.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retrywrites=false&appName=@<account>@
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB cluster connection strings are Mongo-compatible and often use mongodb+srv (SRV) or mongodb schemes; cluster hostnames typically look like <cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com (documentdb-azure-deployment examples) and require TLS (tls=true), SCRAM-SHA-256 authMechanism, and retryWrites=false. The exact host suffix and parameters differ from Cosmos DB's older 'mongo.cosmos.azure.com' endpoints.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Similarity in hostnames and reuse of the 'mongo' / 'cosmos.azure.com' suffix in older Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU) endpoints; the new managed mongoClusters use a different host naming convention and may prefer SRV endpoints.

confusion_sources.title: Cosmos DB MongoDB endpoint examples (older docs)

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong host suffix/port or omitting required TLS/auth parameters (or leaving retryWrites enabled) can cause driver connection failures (authentication errors, protocol negotiation failures) and subtle runtime errors.
improvements: On the connection-strings section of the quickstart and the docdb-connection skill, include the exact SRV and non-SRV example strings for mongoClusters and call out 'use mongodb+srv for SRV endpoints when provided; do not assume :10255 hostnames from older Cosmos DB docs.'

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Azure Cosmos DB is billed primarily by RUs or serverless; vCore offerings exist for some Cosmos features but production model is RUs or serverless.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (the vCore / mongoClusters offering) is provisioned and billed by compute tiers (M10..M200, examples M30 default for prod) and storage; it is a vCore-based model (not RU-based).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The older Cosmos DB (RU) model and the newly renamed vCore offering both live in the broader Microsoft.DocumentDB namespace; the model conflated the RU model with the vCore DocumentDB offering.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumed RUs, they might design throughput and throttling logic incorrectly and choose the wrong service APIs for provisioning; cost and scaling behaviour would not match the actual target cluster.
improvements: Document a short 'billing and capacity' table on the quickstart landing page that contrasts vCore (DocumentDB) vs RU/serverless (Cosmos DB) for MongoDB workloads and links to pricing pages.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: For the MongoDB-compatible API you authenticate with account keys / database user credentials; Microsoft Entra ID is not available for the MongoDB API.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports native SCRAM credentials (user/password) and also supports Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) authentication for the service (documentdb templates and user APIs include MicrosoftEntraID identity provider and the service supports RBAC).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cosmos DB Mongo API historically limited Azure AD integration; the newer DocumentDB / mongoClusters API includes Microsoft Entra ID support and a users resource (identityProvider: MicrosoftEntraID) which the model overlooked.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes only key-based SCRAM auth, they may not implement recommended Entra-based authentication and RBAC; missing Entra ID guidance can result in insecure setups or incorrect credential handling.
improvements: Add an explicit 'Authentication options' subsection to the quickstart that lists SCRAM credentials and Microsoft Entra ID support with a tiny code example or pointer to the 'mongoClusters/users' reference.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use standard MongoDB drivers (for Node.js use the mongodb driver or Mongoose). There is no separate data-plane, Mongo-wire-specific Cosmos SDK.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use standard MongoDB drivers (Mongoose on top of mongodb for Node). Use the documentdb-driver and documentdb-connection skills for driver-specific tuning; management operations use Azure control-plane SDKs only.

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically the MongoDB-compatible API did not expose native vector-index types; no documented createIndex form for HNSW/IVF/DiskANN on Mongo API.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports vector indexes (DiskANN, HNSW, IVF) on paid tiers and provides specific create-index and query patterns (documentdb-vector-search skill describes index creation and query stages). Vector search is supported and the skill documents the commands and parameters to create those indexes.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB at a glance (vector notes)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The Mongo API on Cosmos DB historically lacked vector features; the new DocumentDB vCore offering exposes vector indexes in the DocumentDB engine, and the model defaulted to older Cosmos- or third-party patterns.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes no vector indexes, they may attempt costly external search integrations or miss the simpler single-cluster vector query path.
improvements: Add a 'vector index quick example' to the Vector Search skill and the main quickstart, with a exact createSearchIndexes/createIndex sample and a short HNSW/DiskANN example.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Use Azure Cognitive Search or push data out; the Mongo API does not expose integrated full-text/hybrid search features.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB offers integrated full-text search via createSearchIndexes and the $search aggregation stage (documentdb-full-text-search skill). It supports BM25 queries, fuzzy search, hybrid combinations of lexical and vector retrieval, and the service prefers createSearchIndexes + $search for advanced scenarios rather than using an external Azure Cognitive Search pipeline.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historically, users used Azure Cognitive Search for Cosmos DB search scenarios; the DocumentDB product now integrates advanced search and hybrid (text+vector) capabilities into the engine, and the model defaulted to older patterns.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses an external search service unnecessarily, they may add needless ETL, increased latency, and higher cost compared to the integrated $search approach.
improvements: Add a short 'When to use integrated search vs Cognitive Search' note on the full-text-search quickstart to reduce decision friction.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Supports specific server versions historically (3.2..4.4); many features missing; exact mapping must be confirmed per account.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 (serverVersion property on mongoClusters). Many Mongo operators are supported; compatibility matrices and a feature-operator checklist reside in the 'compatibility' docs. Some rarely-used operators remain unsupported (see the compatibility page for operator-level detail).
confusions.grounding_source: learn.microsoft.com compatibility pages and mongoClusters serverVersion docs

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model reflected older Cosmos DB Mongo API versioning and uncertainty; DocumentDB exposes newer Mongo server versions and documents explicit compatibility matrices which the cold answer did not reference.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes a lower Mongo version, they may avoid using supported aggregation stages or newer features; conversely, assuming unsupported operators will cause runtime errors. The compatibility matrix must be checked for each operator used.
improvements: Add a short 'supported MongoDB server versions' table to the quickstart that lists 5.0, 6.0, 7.0, 8.0 and links to the operator compatibility matrix.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: Use Cosmos DB emulator for SQL/Core API (doesn't emulate Mongo); run local MongoDB docker (mongo:6) on 27017 for development.
confusions.grounded_answer: For Azure DocumentDB development the recommended local approach is the DocumentDB Gateway Docker image (documentdb-local-deployment skill); the gateway image exposes Mongo on port 10260 by default and includes TLS and SCRAM-SHA-256 configuration to mimic the cloud cluster. Running a plain mongo:6 image is a workable alternative for basic driver tests, but the DocumentDB gateway gives closer parity.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The standard Cosmos DB emulator does not implement the DocumentDB vCore semantics; the model fell back to recommending a generic local MongoDB rather than the provided DocumentDB gateway image which is the recommended developer accelerator.
confusions.build_risk: Using plain mongo:6 misses DocumentDB-specific behavior (auth, special index types, vector/search features) and may allow APIs that the real cluster blocks — tests may pass locally but fail in the cloud.
improvements: Document the gateway docker image + exact run command (port 10260, TLS, SCRAM configs) in the local-deployment quickstart and add a developer convenience script to start it.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically Cosmos DB offered Change Feed for Core API; MongoDB-style change streams support has been limited or unavailable in many releases; verify per account.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB change streams and standard driver .watch() usage. For multishard clusters there is a feature toggle to enable 'Change streams for multishard clusters' in the cluster settings; otherwise change streams work with the standard driver and require standard resume token handling and robust error/reconnect logic.

grounding_links.title: Use Mongoose with Azure DocumentDB: Build a Node.js inventory API
Migrate with online migration (change streams noted)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historically Cosmos DB's Mongo API lagged on change-stream compatibility; the new DocumentDB product documents change stream support and any multishard feature toggle, but the model defaulted to older limitations.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming change streams are unavailable would force the builder to use polling or other patterns; incorrectly enabling a migration relying on change streams without the multishard feature configured would fail for sharded clusters.
improvements: Add an example in the Mongoose quickstart that shows Model.watch() plus the note about enabling 'Change streams for multishard clusters' in Settings for sharded clusters.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: The documentdb MCP server contains DocumentDB/Cosmos DB-specific tools (documentdb MCP). The general azure MCP server covers ARM but documentdb server provides data-plane inspection.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the 'documentdb' MCP server is the data-plane toolset (documentdb_list_databases, documentdb_create_index, documentdb_explain_operation, etc.). The 'azure' MCP server is the control-plane server for Azure resource management but does not replace the documentdb data-plane operations.
confusions.grounding_source: machine inventory and documentdb MCP tooling

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Microsoft's original hosted JSON DB was called DocumentDB; it evolved and was rebranded into Azure Cosmos DB. This is unrelated to AWS DocumentDB or open-source DocumentDB.
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly incorrect: 'Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)' was previously named 'vCore-based Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB' and has been rebranded to Azure DocumentDB; this new name distinguishes it from Cosmos DB's RU-based MongoDB API and from the original 2014–2017 'DocumentDB' product (which became Cosmos DB). Azure DocumentDB is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine (governed by the Linux Foundation) and is distinct from Amazon DocumentDB.
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn FAQ and 'What is Azure DocumentDB' pages

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)?
Azure DocumentDB FAQ (relation to Cosmos DB)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Multiple historical rebrandings and similar product names (DocumentDB → Cosmos DB; vCore Cosmos DB for MongoDB → Azure DocumentDB) plus the existence of Amazon DocumentDB create overlapping naming that confuses model memory.

confusion_sources.title: Historical Microsoft Doc referencing DocumentDB → Cosmos DB

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong historical mental model can lead to following incorrect provisioning instructions (targeting the wrong resource type) or miscommunicating with customers about migration paths.
improvements: Add a concise 'Naming and history' callout at the top of the Azure DocumentDB quickstart that lists the previous names and the distinction from Cosmos DB (RU) and Amazon DocumentDB.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: The underlying engine is Azure Cosmos DB's proprietary engine that implements the MongoDB protocol; application code uses standard MongoDB drivers but must be aware of Cosmos DB differences.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore) is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine (governed by the Linux Foundation) built on PostgreSQL for some storage components; it implements the MongoDB wire protocol and provides high compatibility. Applications should use standard MongoDB drivers with minor compatibility checks (see the compatibility matrix).
confusions.grounding_source: What is Azure DocumentDB and release/at-a-glance pages

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)?

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model conflated the older Cosmos DB engine and the newer open-source DocumentDB engine; the earlier Cosmos DB product had proprietary internals while the new DocumentDB product is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming a proprietary Cosmos-only engine may cause the builder to avoid features the open-source engine exposes (vector indexes, search), or to use incorrect migration instructions.
improvements: Add a single sentence near the top of the quickstart that states: 'Azure DocumentDB runs on the open-source DocumentDB engine (MIT) — application code uses Mongo drivers unchanged except where the compatibility guide notes differences.'

confusions.question: What TTL index definition will the sample use to expire cleaning-state documents automatically?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a TTL index on a date field (cleaningExpiresAt) with expireAfterSeconds: 0; set cleaningExpiresAt to new Date(Date.now() + timeoutMs).
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB supports TTL indexes and index options including expireAfterSeconds. The common patterns are: (a) a TTL index on an explicit Date field (e.g., cleaningExpiresAt) with expireAfterSeconds:0 and setting that Date to the expiry instant, or (b) using per-document/container TTL features. Creating a TTL index with expireAfterSeconds on a Date field is supported; validate the cluster's TTL behavior in a quick test because the service also supports _ts-based TTL patterns in some compatibility flows.
confusions.grounding_source: learn TTL and indexing docs (Manage indexing / Time-to-live pages)

grounding_links.title: Manage indexing in Azure DocumentDB (index properties & TTL)
Expire data with Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB and per-document TTL

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes only _ts TTL behavior, they might forget to set the Date field; test per-document TTL on the target cluster to confirm expiry timing.

confusions.question: How will the Node.js Mongoose service open a change stream to detect status transitions?
confusions.cold_answer: Use mongoose.connection.collection('beds').watch(pipeline, { fullDocument: 'updateLookup' }) and handle resume tokens and errors.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use the collection.watch() / Model.watch() API with fullDocument: 'updateLookup' if you need the updated doc. Handle resume tokens, errors, and reconnection. For multishard clusters enable the multishard change-streams feature if required (see the Mongoose quickstart notes).

grounding_links.title: Use Mongoose with Azure DocumentDB: Build a Node.js inventory API

confusions.question: How will the app maintain a live occupancy summary document per ward using atomic updates?
confusions.cold_answer: Use atomic update with $inc/$set and upsert on the ward summary doc, example updateOne({wardId},{ $inc:{occupied:delta}, $set:{updatedAt:new Date()} },{upsert:true}).
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use updateOne with $inc/$set and upsert:true to atomically update per-ward summary counts; single-document atomicity ensures counters are updated safely under concurrent change-stream events.
confusions.grounding_source: documentdb-data-modeling and MongoDB atomic update semantics

confusions.question: What database and collection names and environment variable will the sample use?
confusions.cold_answer: Database: sample_healthcare_12. Collections: beds and ward_summaries. Connection URI from DOCUMENTDB_URI env var.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct and intentional: the run environment (skill_md) requires using database sample_healthcare_12; collections 'beds' and 'ward_summaries' are reasonable and align with the prompt; the connection string must be read from DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime (do not commit secrets).

confusions.question: Which exact client and connection options will the sample use in Node.js to connect to DocumentDB (Mongo API)?
confusions.cold_answer: Use mongoose; connect with useNewUrlParser, useUnifiedTopology, tls:true, replicaSet:'globaldb', retryWrites:false, and fullDocument:'updateLookup' for change streams.
confusions.grounded_answer: Mostly correct: use mongoose (compatible version with Node 24 and Mongo server 7/8). Ensure TLS=true, SCRAM-SHA-256 authMechanism as required by the cluster, and set retryWrites=false (DocumentDB does not support retryable writes). Use fullDocument:'updateLookup' for change streams and follow the singleton MongoClient pattern (documentdb-connection).
confusions.build_risk: If retryWrites remains true, driver may attempt retryable writes causing errors; ensure retryWrites=false in the connection string or options.

information_gaps.title: Seed data & run/test steps
information_gaps.description: The prompt does not supply an idempotent seed script or exact sample seed documents and there is no skill resource that contains a ready-made seed for this sample. The builder must author a seed script (few wards, 5–10 beds each) and a README with exact npm scripts; looked in documentdb-local-deployment and tutorial examples but found no sample_healthcare_12 seed.

information_gaps.title: Exact TTL field semantics in target cluster
information_gaps.description: Although DocumentDB supports TTL indexes and expireAfterSeconds, the docs sometimes emphasise _ts-based TTL for certain Cosmos-compatible flows; the builder should run a quick verification on the target cluster to ensure a TTL on an arbitrary Date field (cleaningExpiresAt with expireAfterSeconds:0) behaves as expected in that account. Looked in manage indexing and TTL docs — supported, but recommended to verify on the live cluster.

information_gaps.title: Presence of DOCUMENTDB_URI env var
information_gaps.description: The run environment statement claims DOCUMENTDB_URI is set in the environment; no installed tool confirms that value. The builder must confirm that DOCUMENTDB_URI is present and points to the intended cluster before running the sample.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Deploy or inspect resources using the Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters resource type (Bicep / az resource create) — do not use Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts or az cosmosdb commands for the vCore DocumentDB clusters.
Use standard MongoDB drivers (Mongoose) to access the cluster and set tls=true, authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256, and retryWrites=false; follow the singleton MongoClient pattern per documentdb-connection.
Implement per-ward summary updates using atomic updateOne with $inc and upsert:true to maintain counters safely from change-stream events.

Expire cleaning-state documents with a TTL index on a Date field (e.g., createIndex({ cleaningExpiresAt: 1 }, { expireAfterSeconds: 0 })) and set cleaningExpiresAt to the desired expiry instant; validate expiry on the target cluster before relying on deletion timing.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Open change streams with collection.watch() or Model.watch() and use fullDocument:'updateLookup'; handle resume tokens and reconnect/retry logic; enable the multishard change-streams feature if you target a sharded cluster and need cross-shard change streams.

inventory_recommendations.name: azd
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this Node/Mongoose sample. If the team later standardizes on the Azure Developer CLI for full-stack deployments, install azd per Microsoft docs (https://learn.microsoft.com/cli/azure/azd).

inventory_recommendations.name: bicep
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Install Bicep on PATH to validate and iterate Bicep templates locally (documentdb-azure-deployment recommends Bicep). Easiest: 'az bicep install' (see Azure Bicep docs).

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: If you want to produce Terraform examples or test Terraform flows, install Terraform on PATH. The documentdb-azure-deployment skill includes Terraform examples.

inventory_recommendations.name: dotnet
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for a Node.js sample. If .NET samples are later added to the repo, install dotnet runtime/sdk via Microsoft docs.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Install mongosh for quick interactive checks of collections and indexes (or add it to PATH); otherwise use the documentdb MCP server's documentdb_find_documents / documentdb_list_indexes tools as the workaround.
